speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: TABLING OF CONVENTION ON PSYCHOTROPIC SUBSTANCES-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 41(2) may I lay on the table of the House, in both official languages, copies of the Convention on Psychotropic Substances which was adopted by the United Nations Conference at the conclusion of its work a few days ago in Vienna.
In view of the pending final report of the Commission of Inquiry into the Non-Medical Use of Drugs, Canada did not sign the convention. However, it is hoped that at some future date hon. members will have the opportunity to discuss the advisability of signing and ratifying this important document.
As hon. members are aware, the conference was called to provide the international community with a legal instrument for the effective control of psychotropic substances, including hallucinogens, stimulants and depressants, which are being increasingly used and abused in many parts of the world. Hon. members will be pleased to hear that the Canadian delegation took an active part in the development of the convention.
I will not attempt to summarize the document in detail. However, I wish to point out that the main thrust of the convention is toward international recognition of the need for rigorous measures to restrict the use of psychotropic substances to legitimate purposes. The convention, however, recognizes that the use of these substances is indispensable for medical and scientific purposes, and that their availability for legitimate use should not be unduly restricted.
In general, the convention envisages levels of control similar to those already in effect in Canada. It was for this reason that the Canadian delegation was able to make such an effective contribution to the work of the conference which led to the development of this important international legal instrument.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT, BARLEY AND OATS FOR 1971-72 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
I wish to inform the House of the level of initial

payments for wheat, barley and oats which will become effective for purchases by the Canadian Wheat Board for the crop year beginning August 1, 1971. For wheat, the basic grade for the new crop year will be the new grade, No. 1 Canada Western Red Spring Wheat, which will replace the present grades of No. 1 Hard and No.l and No. 2 Northern. The initial payment for No. 1 Canada Western Red Spring Wheat for the 1971-72 crop year will be $1.46 per bushel. This is the same as the initial payment for No. 2 Northern in the present crop year.
The initial payment for No. 2 Canada Western Six Row Barley will be 91 cents per bushel, the same level as in effect from August 1 to March 1 of the present crop year.
The initial payment for No. 2 Canada Western Oats will be 60 cents per bushel, the same as the initial payment for the present crop year.
All initial payments are basis in store, Thunder Bay. This early announcement is part of our effort to give the maximum amount of information to producers prior to seeding time.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT, BARLEY AND OATS FOR 1971-72 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, western Canada will of course welcome any type of announcement with regard to at least the initial payments on the three major grains which are under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board.
The other day, however, in releasing the quota arrangements which will go into effect, the department stated that each farmer would have to assign certain fixed acreages for the coming crop year. I note that in the statement released today certain total volumes of wheat, barley and oats are shown and the Wheat Board has indicated it will take in approximately 388 million bushels of wheat, 230 million bushels of barley and 45 million bushels of oats. It is difficult for a farmer to assign any particular acreage if he does not know what the delivery quota will be on a bushel per acre basis. We have a situation in which we have two unknowns and only one known up until now. We cannot figure out an algebraic formula in which there are two unknowns and only one known and come up with a correct answer.
Unless the government is ready at this particular time to indicate what it means in terms of bushels per acre the announcements to date do not make too much sense. Farmers may feel that they have sufficient grain for a six-bushel delivery quota, but if more farmers take advantage of the 388 million bushels of wheat that will be taken in they may find themselves in the position of facing a four-bushel quota and as a result will lose some of their assignable acreage.
The 388 million bushels that the Wheat Board has indicated will be taken in does not fulfil the initial promise made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that the government would set its sights on a total of approximately 1,200 million bushels of wheat to be sold over a three-year period. In addition to the price of wheat being lowered, reflecting a comparison with No. 2 wheat last
March 1, 1971

year, the price of barley is again lowered to the level it was prior to March 1. Even although from March 1 to the end of the current crop year the government seems to be providing some incentive to farmers to make deliveries, I suggest the lowering of the price offers no inducement to them to do so next year.
The announcement also indicates that the government is somewhat reluctant to provide incentives to farmers to produce feed grain, a commodity that we sadly lack in terms of the export market. There was also one other indication-

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENTS FOR WHEAT, BARLEY AND OATS FOR 1971-72 CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what the minister's statement means to the western grain farmer is that not only will the initial price of wheat not be increased but it will in fact drop some four cents a bushel, and barley will be at the same level. I think this assessment is a fair reflection of the questions that have been put to the minister repeatedly during the last week or two about the International Grains Arrangement. As a result of the failure of the price negotiations, I think the government's announcement is an indication of what our farmers can look forward to in the international market in terms of price.
What the lowering of the initial price of wheat by four cents a bushel and the restoration of the initial price of barley to its previous level, with the exception of a small increase of ten cents in the current crop year, means to the farmers is that a really tough competitive position is facing them in the export market in the coming crop year. We should have liked the minister to state clearly in the extra information he gave just how competitive we can expect the export market to be. Certain volumes of wheat and barley have been mentioned, but we do not know just how tough we will have to be in competing with the United States, which according to United States Department of Agriculture reports is increasing acreages of corn, sorghum, barley and spring wheat this year. For example, they are projecting an increase of some 17 per cent for spring wheat. This means we have not received any co-operation in cutting down on acreage and that we are going to be in a tough, competitive market. The real question the farmers are asking is, are they going to get volume.
We still do not know what will be the outcome of the minister's proposed stabilization program. Perhaps he is

still negotiating with the farm organizations to see whether they will accept all or part of what he has put before them. Does this delay in any announcement regarding the stabilization program indicate a lack of acceptance by farmers and farm organizations in western Canada? These are questions which are left unanswered by the minister's statement today. We still have to await the outcome of the talks he is having to find out what the government's price stabilization program is really going to be.
I welcome his announcement today on initial prices as it will at least give the farmers a clear indication of where they are going.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prairie farmers will have been especially encouraged-if I can use that word-during the last week in February, because for the second time, a minister has announced amendments to the initial prices to be paid for grain, provided of course that it is stored in Thunder Bay.
Previously, it had been announced that an amount of $40 million would be allotted to a program aimed at encouraging western farmers to devote themselves to fodder growing.
I must say that in eastern Canada, there is an exceedingly serious problem. During the weekend, farmers and agricultural organizations have again made to me representations to the effect that they are still encountering difficulties in obtaining feed grain and that prices are constantly increasing.
Even though prices might be somewhat higher in the East, I hope the western farmers will benefit by it, although it seems from the statements I have just heard that it will not be so.
In any event, I would again ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) to see to it that the eastern farmers are able to get feed grain at better conditions, by increasing grants to transportation if necessary, because at the present time many hog, broiler and even egg producers are on the verge of bankruptcy. We seem to be heading towards utter confusion.
Over the weekend I heard that the Quebec Minister of Agriculture wanted to built a slaughter-house in the Quebec area so as to encourage the farmers who had to give up dairy production to switch to hog production; grants would be paid to them, so that the land that was used for the production of fodder could now serve for the production of grain, thus enabling them to feed their pigs at lower cost.
In the West, farmers are told to stop growing grain and to grow fodder. In the East, they are told to do the opposite. And that, in the same country.
Mr. Speaker, it will be necessary to come to an agreement, to sit down and seriously discuss, in one and the same country, the best programs to be carried out, in order to ensure to both the eastern and the western farmers, better conditions and their fair share of the national revenue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Louis-Roland Comeau (South Western Nova) moved:
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext:
That Bill C-2. to amend the Canada Shipping Act, be. amended by inserting the following in Clause 2 immediately after line 18 at page 1:
"(d) "discharge" includes, but not so as to limit its meaning, any spilling, leaking, pumping, pouring, emitting, emptying, sifting or dumping."
and by relettering subsequent paragraphs accordingly.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the amendment is very simple, and I do not intend to speak on it at great length. This amendment merely defines the word "discharge".
The side note to clause 7 of the bill, as reprinted and reported from the committee, simply reads "Discharges of Pollutants". The word "discharge" appears five times in that clause. I move this amendment because the word "discharge" is not defined in the definition section or anywhere else in the bill. I intended to move this amendment in committee because several people were interested in this definition. We know what happened. The bill went through clause by clause on a day when I was not present in committee.
As I mentioned, the word "discharge" is not defined in section 736, the definition section of the Act. I realize that the oil pollution prevention regulations in Canada define the word "discharge", but it is not a very accurate definition for our purposes. In the oil pollution prevention regulations, the word "discharge" is defined as:
"discharge" in relation to a pollutant means any discharge or escape howsoever caused or occurring.
My amendment follows the wording of the United States water quality improvement act passed April 3, 1970. According to the act, "discharge" includes but is not limited to, any spilling, leaking, pumping, pouring, emitting, emptying or dumping. This definition is better than
Canada Shipping Act
the one proposed in our oil pollution prevention regulations. On that basis, with some alterations, I move this amendment. Although this is a very minor amendment, the word "discharge" should be clearly defined so that we will know exactly what is meant. If the government does not like my definition, or prefers its own definition of the word "discharge', I submit an amendment should be brought in so Canadian ship owners or cargo owners may know exactly what is meant. Many of the witnesses who appeared before the committee expressed the desire that a definition be included in the bill. I am glad to see the minister here this afternoon. The bulk of the department's evidence before the committee was given by Mr. Macgillivray, Director of Marine Regulations Branch. For a while he was unwilling to accept many changes in the minister's absence; this was probably the reason the definition for which I am asking has not been included.
I realize the measure has to be a strong one. The minister has indicated time and time again that the department is taking a tough line. In these circumstances, it is only fair we should let the companies know exactly what is in store for them. The bill is of great concern to international interests as well as to purely Canadian concerns. Certain countries, particularly Scandinavian countries and Britain, have, I understand, expressed some concern about the terms of the bill. It is important, therefore, that the standards set must be clearly set out before the legislation becomes operative.
I am sure that had I been present on the day the committee discussed this particular clause the government would have accepted the amendment I have put forward. I trust the government will do so now, or, if not, at least insert some definition of the word "discharge".

speechtext:
I move:
That Bill C-2, An Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act, be amended by inserting the following in Clause 2 immediately after line 20 at page 2:
"(g) "Minister", notwithstanding anything in any other Part, means the Minister of the Environment;" and by relettering subsequent paragraphs accordingly.
As stated by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose), this is a bi-partisan amendment. I suggest we consider the amendment in light of what took place in the committee of the whole the other day during the debate on the clean air bill. In response to a point of order raised at that time, Your Honour ruled that we were not prevented from including the expression "minister of the environment" in that bill by what had happened during debate on the government organization bill. I assume that the government is going ahead with its proposal, and if this amendment is accepted as well as the amendment of the hon. member for St. John's East to the government organization bill, then I suspect a new amendment can be brought in at a later date.
We have been saying for some time that all matters relating to pollution control should be brought under the one roof. The minister who will be responsible for antipollution measures is the minister of the environment, whoever he may be. This amendment simply gives the new minister of the environment control over all legislation-excepting the Arctic waters bill-dealing with pollution control.
In this respect, it is consistent with what we have been arguing for some time. For over a year now we have been arguing that this be done. We made the point when we debated the Canada Water Act last year; we repeated it this year when studying various anti-pollution measures. However, the government, in the actions it has taken this year, has reversed its stand from the position it took when we discussed the Canada Water Act.
We do not dislike the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson); let me say that at the outset. We like the minister and think he will do a good job. On the other hand, we do think it essential that one minister be made responsible for all anti-pollution measures. At the present time there is a multiplicity of jurisdictions with regard to pollution control, and for this reason one minister should look after the interests of the environment.
The new minister should be responsible for controlling oil pollution, which is one of the greatest threats at the present time to the environment, especially the fishery. Since the new minister of the environment will have jurisdiction over the fishery and will be relieving the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources of its jurisdiction over certain sections of water, it seems to me the prevention of oil pollution should also be made the responsibility of the minister of the environment. This is the reason for the amendment I have now proposed.
The new regulations pursuant to this new Canada Shipping Act will be made to apply to any fishing zones in Canada prescribed pursuant to the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act. This underlines my contention that the pollution control to which I referred should be

March 1, 1971

brought under one roof. Many of the departmental officials who will apply the legislation will be from the Department of Transport, but at the same time over-all jurisdiction over oil pollution in this context should, it seems to me, be within the department of the minister who protects the environment, and particularly the fisheries. Of greatest interests in this regard is the fishery. This bill makes provision respecting both the Atlantic and west coast fisheries, which are our greatest fishing resources, though it also applies to the Great Lakes as well. Since there must be very close liaison between the department of fisheries and the administrators of this new act, it seems to me that the minister of the environment should be responsible for both aspects.
Last year's throne speech was heralded with great fanfare as the anti-pollution throne speech because the government was proposing to set up a new department to protect the environment. For once, the government was going to start to tackle the pollution problem and to place responsibility upon one minister. I should like to know why the government does not wish the new minister of the environment to have complete control of all anti-pollution measures. I do not understand why the government excepts the Arctic waters anti-pollution bill that Parliament passed last year, because that measure also relates to pollution control. Although the government may have some explanation, it does seem to me that responsibility for controlling pollution should be with this new department. The interests of the fisheries are very much at stake here. The movement of oil, as well as the movement of other pollutants, must be very much in the mind of the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis). If the movement of pollutants, other than oil, is to be authorized this has to be a matter of concern. Last year the movement of phosphorus through Canadian waters was of great concern to the minister.
To be consistent with what our party has been trying to do, and what the government has been trying to do, it seems to me that all parties in the House should accept this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, the argument advanced by the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) in support of his amendment was very much along the lines I expected. I find myself basically in agreement with the argument he has presented. I am sure Your Honour has heard my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), pursue the same theme in his speeches. The amendment I intend to propose will add additional words to the motion presented by the hon. member. Inasmuch as the amendment ends with the word "environment" I find myself very much tempted to add the words "and fisheries". This would be in line with what the hon. member had in mind when he suggested withdrawing his amendment. However, I thought I might be anticipating another debate, so should refrain from inserting these words at this point.
As the hon. member has suggested, the consequential changes arising from this proposed change of name might be dealt with at a later date. I do not intend to
Canada Shipping Act
repeat the arguments which have been advanced in support of this basic idea, but I do want to say at once that I am concerned with some of the implications of this amendment. If one examines the terms of the bill, which sets out the responsibilities of the new ministry of environment, he will agree that this amendment is a step in the direction some of us have been advocating. The minister of environment should have general jurisdiction or supervision over activities of the government which directly affect the environment, that is the taking of appropriate steps to prevent further pollution of that environment.
In most respects, the bill we have before us is primarily concerned with the matter of shipping and the construction of ships. It is concerned with the type of navigational equipment they will carry and the rules under which they will operate. For this reason, it does seem to me that any addition to the Canada Shipping Act most appropriately rests in the hands of our Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), who generally has responsibility for administering this act. The fact that the thrust and purport of this bill is directed toward the prevention of pollution indicates the minister of environment should also have some authority at least to designate what levels of pollution will be acceptable for the purposes of this act and how pollutants will be defined. There are certain clauses of the bill which relate specifically to this aspect of the matter. They have to do with the carrying of oil and other pollutants in bulk cargoes.
It seems to me there is a happy point of compromise between the position set out in the bill, which would put the new part of the shipping act entirely under the minister's jurisdiction, and the position outlined by the member for South Western Nova in his amendment. If one were to follow through with the hon. member's argument, he would revert to the days when we had a department of marine and fisheries. In those days what is now the Department of Transport looked after shipping as well as fisheries. Surely, the hon. member does not want to revert to that situation. In this day and age I would not advocate this move, and I doubt very much if the minister, in view of his responsibilities regarding air transport, railways and a few other minor things like that, would welcome the idea of again having within his jurisdiction the department of fisheries.
I have sought to come up with something which separates the basically sound idea of the hon. member for South Western Nova and what to me seems to be the logic of having the Minister of Transport responsible for those things referred to in the bill. Therefore, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Surrey (Mr. Mather):
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom the semicolon following the word "Environment", and by inserting the words,
"for the purposes of Section 737, subsection (1) and Section 739, subsection (1), paragraphs (a) and (m), and the Minister shall recommend to the Governor in Council any regulations proposed to be made pursuant thereto;"

March 1, 1971
Canada Shipping Act The amendment would then read:
That Bill C-2, an Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act, be amended by inserting the following in Clause 2 immediately after line 20 at page 2:
"(g) 'Minister', notwithstanding anything in any other Part, means the Minister of the Environment for purposes of Section 737, subsection (1) and Section 739, subsection (1), paragraphs
(a)	and (m), and the Minister shall recommend to the Governor in Council any regulations proposed to be made pursuant thereto;" and by relettering subsequent paragraphs accordingly.
Let me take a moment to draw attention to the particular subsections I have in mind. Proposed section 737 is headed "Discharges of Pollutants". Proposed subsection (1) reads:
The Governor in Council may make regulations prohibiting the discharge from ships of any one or more pollutants specified in the regulations, except as thereby authorized, in any waters to which this Part applies and with respect to which those regulations are made applicable.
Proposed section 739(1) is fairly lengthy. It sets out the authorization for a number of regulations, most of which have entirely to do with the question of regulating of ships, that is the type of navigational equipment and so on they are required to carry. But paragraph (a) of subsection 1 provides that regulations may be made prescribing substances and classes of substances that are, for the purposes of this part, pollutants. It would seem to me that this part deals very specifically with an area of the responsibility of the proposed department of the environment. In practice under my proposal as I see it, if regulations are to be drafted the minister of the environment would have to say, before the draft is presented to the governor in council for enactment, that the regulations are in conformity with the general type of regulations we are developing to control pollutants. This department will have to decide what are pollutants under the terms of other acts whether the Fisheries Act, the Water Act or any of perhaps a number of other acts.
When we come to paragraph (m) of subsection (1), we find it provides that regulations are to be made for regulating and preventing the pollution of air by ships. Here, it would seem to me we are moving directly into an area of responsibility that is within the ambit of the proposed clean air bill. If the minister of the environment, as is proposed, is to be the responsible minister in respect of the administration of the clean air act, then here again is an area of responsibility which this legislation should properly allocate to the minister of the environment so that he will have a voice at some point prior to any administrative responsibility being turned over to the Minister of Transport.
It would seem to me that the proposal I have put forward represents a logical step in the legislative process to ensure that the will of Parliament, which has been referred to in many speeches made in this House, is emphasized at the present time. I believe there has been general support so far for the basic concept of the clean air bill, and indeed for the establishment of a department
of the environment no matter what the particular name might be. Therefore, I believe these proposals would be consistent with the wish expressed generally in Parliament as to the approach we should be taking and the concept which, in principle, now is obviously accepted by both sides of the House. It seems to me we should start tying in very specifically the responsibility of the minister of the environment, as it has been outlined in the proposals for the department, with the various acts which are to be under his administration. One of those acts should be this one which, while generally speaking is within the ambit of the administration of ships and the rules of navigation, ties in closely with the general question of helping to preserve an environment which is fit for us to live in.

Order, please. The point raised by the hon. member, of course, is of interest. As he said, some time ago, after the new rules were accepted by the House, a point was raised as to whether it was possible to amend a motion at the report stage. At that time, the Chair ruled it was possible to make such an amendment, but that amendments at this stage are subject to the same rules and limitations as amendments at other stages. I am not sure I can interpret the amendment proposed now by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) in the same way the hon. member does. My interpretation of the motion proposed by the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) is that the minister, for the purposes of the Canada Shipping Act, would be the minister of the environment. The hon. member suggested this applied only to part IX. There could be an interesting legal question concerning what the minister of the environment, or whatever he may be called, should have jurisdiction over under the Canada Shipping Act.
It seems to me the amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett), from a procedural stand-
[Mr. Barnett.)
March 1, 1971

point, is very helpful because it indicates exactly what was in the motion presented by the hon. member for South Western Nova. I would think the point raised by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), as he says, perhaps is academic to some extent. There will always be some difficulty in determining what is acceptable by way of a proposed amendment to a motion moved at the report stage. It will never be easy to make such a decision. I recognize the importance of the point raised by the hon. member for Peace River, but I do not think the matter should be pressed further. speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):

speechtext:
It
has been a most interesting discussion and a very enlightening one in view of your ruling, Mr. Speaker. Since we have spent so much time arguing about the legality or propriety of both the motion and the amendment, now that the matter has been resolved it pains me somewhat to say that, personally, I cannot accept either one of them. I understand fully and sympathize with the principle that has been espoused by the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau), that is the concept of having all pollution matters within some form of centralized control. I take it that the other hon. member who moved the amendment to the motion had something of the same nature in mind. However, it does seem to me that we do not do any offence to the basic concept of a centralized form of control if in a sense we separate it into two parts, that is those parts of the control which are exercised through legislative authority such as is contained in the various environmental bills, and second, the kind of co-ordinating authority which undoubtedly will be present in so far as this measure is concerned, as well as a great many more.
The proposal as put forward by the hon. member for South Western Nova is one we examined in great detail, that is the department under which this part of the act would be most appropriate. I can assure the hon. member

and indeed this was discussed at some length in committee-that the judgment we made was not one which reflected any proprietary interest on my part or any feeling that once having acquired some form of responsibility it would be sinful to dispose of it in any other way. It was a very practical judgment and one that I think is entirely defensible. This is a small but important part of the total responsibility for the administration and control of shipping, both in Canadian waters and as it applies to the hundreds of aspects of the Canada Shipping Act. It is perfectly clear that in terms of the sections with regard to pollution matters and the like, the expertise and the capability repose in the Department of Transport. It is also evident, I think, from events of the past year or so that we have quite the best capability that exists at the present time for dealing with pollution incidents of this kind. I would not want to argue that our capability is by any means 100 per cent, far from it. I have indicated on several occasions that there is a great deal more to be learned about this subject. Nevertheless, it is my judgment, supported I believe by the evidence, that this measure and the responsibility for carrying it out, rests best at this moment within the Department of Transport.
One or two other illustrations may help to reinforce my contention. For example, it is clear that the coastguard will have to play a major role in terms of carrying out these responsibilities. If there were to be divided

March 1, 1971
Canada Shipping Act
jurisdiction in the manner which the hon. member suggests, then it is conceivable that valuable time would be lost in the event of a pollution spill or something of that nature with which we had to cope.
I think the essential argument is that, comparatively speaking, this is a small part of the total Canada Shipping Act. This is not by any means a precedent, and indeed hon. members on all sides of the House agreed with proposals which I put forward some months ago and which were supported unanimously with regard, for example, to the emission of exhaust fumes from automobiles. The judgment of hon. members at that time was that even though this had major pollution overtones, nevertheless, because the Department of Transport was the principal agency with regard to the inspection of newly manufactured automobiles and the like, it was most appropriate that this particular provision with regard to the emission levels of exhaust from automobiles should remain within the Department of Transport. This amendment, Mr. Speaker, is designed to deal with a very basic inadequacy in what generally speaking is a very good bill. It proposes that instead of administering the provisions of the bill for a distance 12 miles seaward from our coastlines, the jurisdiction of the administration be extended 100 miles seaward from our coastlines in all of the waters lying south of the sixtieth parallel. In other words, this measure would apply to those waters adjacent to the coasts of Canada that do not lie within the ambit of the Arctic Waters Pollution Control bill which we dealt with in the last session of Parliament.
I said generally speaking this is a very good bill. I think its passage through the standing committee would bear out my contention because there were quite a number of amendments that were generally agreed to in the committee and which were brought forward to this House at the report stage. This proposal of mine did not receive the endorsation of the majority of the committee members and, therefore, I bring it forward for the consideration of the House today.
I have in my hand a clipping from the Victoria Colonist of August 9, 1970 which has reference to the aftermath of a situation which developed in Active Pass. This is on the shipping route generally used by many of the vessels travelling between the port of Victoria, our capital city in British Columbia, and the Vancouver area. There was a collision in Active Pass between a Russian freighter and a vessel of the B.C. Ferry service, which resulted in very severe damage to the ferry. The ferry was out of service for quite some time for major repairs, and there was also loss of life. It was a serious accident, although I might say not as serious in the context of the bill which we have before us as it would have been if either one or both of the ships had been tankers carrying oil. The U.S.S.R. vessel was a general cargo one, and so no major question of pollution was involved.
I mention this clipping because it reports Federal Transport Minister Don Jamieson as saying that changes in navigation law would have to come before alterations in coastal routes and Vancouver Harbour approaches could be determined.
"We can't instruct a ship or tell a ship where to go under the present law", he said.
The lack in the law referred to by the minister at that time, in my view is the basic gap that the bill with which we are dealing is designed to close. While this bill is one of the more complicated bills that I have studied in committee, I think the essence of it is sound and the general principle is one which the House should support.

So, the area of debate raised by my amendment does not deal with the basic principle of the bill but with the question of the area of its jurisdiction.
I would suggest that in view of a couple of events, this proposal of mine is rather appropriately being discussed today. One is that this is about the time that our proclaimed fishing zones become operative. At least, the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) issued a statement a little while ago that they would become operative as of the end of February. So, we are starting in somewhat of a new era so far as the area over which Canadian jurisdiction for pollution purposes, among other things, applies.

The second event which I suggest makes this discussion appropriate is that this is D-day in the province of British Columbia for the launching of a petition which it is hoped will secure one million signatures from residents of British Columbia and of the State of Washington in the U.S., protesting the proposed establishment of an oil tanker route from the State of Alaska through the Strait of Juan de Fuca to an oil refinery on the mainland of the continental U.S. This event, Mr. Speaker, fits in very well with the suggestion that has been made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) that Canadians should speak out and express their concern about proposals of this kind. I suggest that I am providing the House with an opportunity to speak out on this sort of thing through the amendment that I am proposing.
Much has happened in this fast moving world of ours since the previous session of this House when we passed certain bills that impinge upon some areas of our concern respecting the future of the environment of the country. In the previous session we passed the first Arctic Waters Pollution Control bill and a bill amending the Territorial Seas and Fishing Zones Act which extended our territorial sea to 12 miles from three miles and made possible the application of the fishing zones now in effect on our Atlantic and Pacific coasts. Some of the things which have happened have highlighted the need for the kind of bill with which we are dealing. I am referring to certain events on the Atlantic coast at Chedabucto Bay. Much of the time of the committee was devoted to considering the implications arising from that disaster involving an oil tanker.
More recently there was a double tanker collision in the entrance to San Francisco Harbour under the Golden Gate. Large quantities of oil were poured into the waters of that particular part of the west coast. Even more recently, Mr. Speaker, and closer to home, there was an occurrence in my constituency. At the end of last week a large body of heavy oil was moving inshore at the edge of Long Beach, adjacent to where we have just established our new west coast national marine park. Anyone

March 1, 1971
Canada Shipping Act
who wants an idea of how Long Beach appears need only look at the picture on the cover of this year's British Columbia telephone directory. Although that is the most extensive individual beach in the area, there are many other beautiful beaches that could be affected by this oil. So, we have had fair warning. I hope that the minister, who was not here for the question period, can give us some more detailed information of the size of this body of oil, where it has come from, and any other information of that kind on this point. As I say, we have had fair warning of what may be impending for the Pacific Coast, at least if this route for large tankers carrying oil from the north slope of Alaska down the west coast of Canada is inaugurated.
If anticipated pollution as a result of shipping developing in the Arctic warranted Canada taking action last year to place the 100-mile pollution and territorial seas zone around the Arctic islands, then I suggest the very real and pressing dangers on our Atlantic and Pacific coasts that have been so dramatically demonstrated since the time we passed the Arctic Waters bill warrant and justify, for the sake of our own national survival and safety as a people, the same kind of control with regard to the same kind of use of our waters out to 100 miles. My amendment proposes that. As somebody has said, there is no magic in that particular figure.
I should like to suggest that it ought to be considered a minimum more than a maximum. Anyone who thinks that we are trying to take over control of the oceans of the world should look, I suggest, at a map of the Pacific Ocean and see what a small portion of the Pacific Ocean is encompassed by that area extending 100 miles from our coastline. One can realize this is a very modest suggestion, indeed.
I know that arguments will be advanced that we are going beyond accepted international law, and perhaps we are. Perhaps we are developing what is sometimes called the customary law of states. Yet I suggest to the House that if, in keeping with Canada's place in the world, we proclaimed that 100-mile zone around our Arctic islands, it would be even more in keeping with our place in the world if we were to seek to develop the international law by saying that the same principle applies to our Pacific and to our Atlantic coasts.
We are not completely without grounds in taking this sort of action. Speaking on the second reading of the bill to amend the Territorial Seas and Fishing Zones Act, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, as reported at page 6013 of Hansard for April 17, 1970:
We cannot, however, accept the notion that a coastal state's fisheries conservation and protection jurisdiction must cease at 12 miles from shore.
The developments since 1960 have proved that there is no magic in the 12-mile limit. Unlike the deer and bears in national parks, who become aware after a period that they are safe when they enter the sanctuary of the park, the fish do not seem to know that they are safe-except of course from Canadian fishermen-when they enter the 12-mile limit.
A little later in the same paragraph, the minister said:
Once again, Canada, after long and serious deliberations, has decided to go it alone.
The suggestion, if my amendment means that we are to go it alone, is not without precedent, even if one were to consider actions proposed and taken by the present administration. It is becoming more and more apparent to me every day that, in some respects, we cannot wait for international treaties to come into being.
A good deal of discussion has arisen about the Brussels Conference of late 1969. It was referred to in a statement by professors of international law at the Faculty of Law, University of Toronto, presented at the Annual Conference of the American Society of International Law meeting in New York City on April 24, 1970. The heading of this document is "The Canadian Initiative to Establish a Maritime Zone for Environmental Protection: its Significance for Multilateral Development of International Law". Page 3 of the document, as I have it in typewritten manuscript form, reads:
At the Brussels Conference late in 1969 IMCO drafted a more far-reaching convention.
This is more far-reaching than the original convention on the matter of pollution of the sea by oil.
Even if it is ratified by most of the shipping and coastal nations concerned, it contains the same basic defect of not providing for meaningful preventive regulation. The Canadian delegation at that conference argued in vain for the adoption of an effective regime of environmental protection.
As I understand it, this is what the proposed amendment to the Canada Shipping Act is all about. It is a matter of trying to create an effective regime of environmental protection and meaningful preventive regulation.
I was happy when the committee accepted my suggestion that the reference to pollution control officers in the bill be changed to "pollution prevention officers". As far as I am concerned, the essence of the bill is to seek to develop preventive regulations against the dangers of possible massive oil spills. No matter how effective the measures may be that we may develop in the future under the coastguard, or what kind of materials we stockpile, in some respects they are going to be ineffective once the oil is in the water and moving toward our shore line. I was glad to see the minister make a reference to the emphasis that should be placed upon the coastguard in this role. My constituents on the west coast are getting a sample of the heavy, massive goo that can come ashore on some of the most beautiful sand beaches in the world. What destruction will occur on a large scale if we do not take measures to create effective preventive regulations?
The International Convention Relating to Intervention on the High Seas in Cases of Oil Pollution Casualties is limited in its effect to action that is taken after the event, rather than before. Article I reads:
Parties to the present Convention may take such measures on the high seas as may be necessary to prevent, mitigate or eliminate grave and imminent danger to their coastline or related interests from pollution or threat of pollution of the sea by oil,-
Then, comes the real crux of it:
-following upon a maritime casualty or acts related to such a casualty,-

March 1, 1971

A maritime casualty is defined as meaning a collision, running aground on a reef or other events of that character. The related interests which are included are interesting and relevant. The definition section of Article II reads:
"Related interests" means the interests of a coastal State directly affected or threatened by the maritime casualty, such as:
{a) maritime coastal, port or estuarine activities, including fisheries activities, constituting an essential means of livelihood of the persons concerned;
(b)	tourist attractions of the area concerned;
(c)	the health of the coastal population and the well-being of the area concerned, including conservation of living marine resources and of wildlife;
This is what we are really concerned with in this bill. Basically, we are trying to take steps to prevent the danger of any oil spill on the water, rather than merely dealing with it as a right on the high seas after a marine casualty has occurred. This is an obvious gap in the international agreements. This matter is becoming so pressing that we are at least compelled to make an attempt to take preventive action a reasonable distance from our shores. This point is being driven home to thousands of people on the Pacific coast now that there is a discussion about tankers travelling down our coastline from the state of Alaska.
No one can logically argue that 100 miles is an unreasonable distance from our shores to seek to take preventive action. We are not being unfair with regard to the activities of other nations if we simply say that if they come within a short distance of our shores,-their ships must meet certain standards and have certain navigational aids, obey certain navigational rules and in specific areas follow traffic regulations.
When I spoke on second reading of the bill, I said that 12 miles off our shore was nothing more than spitting distance. I shrink inside when I think of the possibility of the glorious stretch of ocean shore in our new national park, Long Beach, being contaminated in the same way as some areas on the Atlantic coast of Canada were affected by the spill of the Arrow. Those who know about these things have told me that when considering the kind of tanker proposed for service down the coast from Alaska, we must bear in mind that after their engines have been put full speed astern they travel five miles before coming to a stop. In that context, how effective is a 12-mile zone off our coasts? It is obviously not realistic that the jurisdiction of this bill should be limited to such a short distance off our coasts.
The principle of this amendment is exactly the same as the one proposed last year to the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). It was turned down in the committee, as a matter of fact, and ruled out of order in the House. However, it is certainly within the ambit of the bill before us today.
During the debate on the Territorial Seas and Fishing Zones Act last year I proposed an amendment which Would have extended our fishing zones. During that dis-
Canada Shipping Act
cussion, as may be found in Hansard of June 4, 1970, at page 7747, I set out the action which had been taken unilaterally by the United States under President Truman in 1945. I have here a copy of the Presidential Proclamation number 2668 of September 28, 1945 with respect to coastal fisheries in certain parts of the high seas. This reflects President Truman's conviction that there was need for action to preserve fishing resources. In this case, the need was so great that the United States had to make this move on its own initiative in the absence of existing international law or agreement. In other words, the United States was making new law. It was subsequent to this declaration that certain of the South American countries took steps to extend their own fishing zones.

speechtext: Like Peru.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext:
Peru, Ecuador, Chile and now, I understand, Brazil. So, there is an important section of the coastline of South America in respect of which jurisdiction extending 200 miles is claimed and where steps are taken to enforce this jurisdiction. At any rate, since a declaration such as this has been made by our friendly neighbour to the south, on its own initiative, I submit that should this amendment be agreed to the United States could not, with any logic, take objection in these circumstances. They might, of course, say: we can do it because we are big, but you cannot do it, because you are little. I do not believe they are prepared to take such a position; I do not believe the United States is prepared to develop a thesis of that kind, justifying its own actions while condemning ours. I have more faith in the people of the United States than that.
As I have mentioned, the action proposed in the amendment does not conflict with accepted international practice in certain circumstances, that is what some of our constitutional experts have described in the committee as a development of the customary law of states, something which we, according to certain of these experts, did last year in relation to the Arctic. I suggest we ought to do a little more of it this year with respect to the Atlantic and the Pacific. If the concern felt by the United States in 1945 about the conservation of the fisheries and the protection of marine life was real enough to require unilateral action to be taken, how much more pressing is the need today?
My amendment is a fairly long one and I shall not go into all its details. I should like to point out, though, that it has been carefully drafted in order that its provisions should not conflict with the rights of other nations whose waters adjoin our own. This is dealt with in that part of the amendment which refers to the provisions of subsection (4) of Section 5 of the Territorial Seas and Fishing Zones Act which gives the Governor in Council the right to issue the list of geographic co-ordinates in areas where the territorial sea or fishing zones of another country come close to our coasts. In other words, we are not seeking to assert any wider jurisdiction over waters which properly and normally belong to other nations.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs, in answer to questions in the House in recent days concerning the

March 1, 1971
Canada Shipping Act
proposed establishment of a tanker route from Alaska, has on one or two occasions referred to the value of speaking out. On February 18 he said:
I think it is most important that during the period while hearings are being held, Canadians and Americans should realize the potential risks involved and speak out, and speak out clearly.
Again, on February 22, he said:
I do believe it is important that all of those concerned, particularly the people affected in the State of Washington and in the Province of British Columbia, should make their views about this question known so that at least this decision is made in the full knowledge of the very serious danger of pollution which exists. I have no hesitation in saying on behalf of the Canadian government that we believe there are serious dangers *ot pollution.
I agree with the Secretary of State for External Affairs that it would not be appropriate for the Canadian government to appear officially before a board holding hearings in the United States. Nevertheless, the danger of pollution is real and serious and I suggest the time has come not only for the Canadian people as private citizens to speak out, but for this Parliament to take some positive action to recognize the danger which the Secretary of State mentioned in his reply to the questions about the proposed tanker route on the Pacific coast. It is all very well for us to make pious exhortations to citizens; when it comes right down to it, we who sit in this chamber are the only ones who can make the voice of the people effective. It is time to make that voice effective at least to the extent of the amendment I propose, one which would add to the protective jurisdiction of the bill before us.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). I spoke on Bill C-2 when it was introduced on October 26 of last year.
The bill before us deals, in my view, with one of the most important problems facing Canadians, namely, the pollution of our environment. The motion proposed by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is a lengthy one and I shall not burden the House by reading it. I shall refer only to parts of it. Part III deals with fishing zones. I question the value of using the fishing zones in Canada, as the basis of this amendment. I question the value of the wording of this particular amendment, which provides that regulations shall apply to any fishing zones of Canada described pursuant to the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act, because in some cases fishing zones as defined are inoperative.
As the House is well aware, the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act was passed unilaterally with great fanfare in 1964. If the terms of that legislation had been implemented and enforced in that year, or even in 1965, then our fishermen, especially those on the east coast, would not today be facing a serious decline in their fisheries resources due to over-fishing by other countries. However, the legislation was not enforced in 1964, nor in 1965, 1966, 1967, 1968, 1969 or 1970. As a result of the
government's procrastinating attitude haddock have become almost extinct, our herring resources are diminishing, while stocks of redfish, flounder and cod have declined to dangerous levels. The legislation is not enforced to this day on the south coast of Newfoundland.
This amendment is based on fishing zones that are not truly operative, which of course poses the question for the members of this party whether we can support an amendment of this type. Recently the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) made an announcement outside the House with regard to fishing zones, but these, as I said a moment ago, do not apply to the south coast of Newfoundland. Neither do they apply to the area surrounding St. Pierre and Miquelon. As a matter of fact, the minister's announcement only accentuated the problem of defining territorial seas and fishing zones in the area of St. Pierre and Miquelon.
Paragraph (c) of the amendment provides the interesting proposition that the regulations would apply to waters adjacent to the sea coasts of Canada as measured up to 100 miles from the base lines. We believe that this particular Bill should come under the authority of the Minister of Transport, and we express that view because he, in the final analysis, has the right to determine the types of ships that are constructed at the present time. It is for the Minister of Transport to define what should be the strength of oil tanks and water tanks, or the thickness of wood or steel used in the construction of ships in Canada. It is for the minister to make certain that his officials are aware that all ships employ proper navigational aids as required by law.
This is why we believe the Minister of Transport should have jurisdiction over the regulation of pollution control on the high seas. While we agree that steps must be taken not only to see that pollution is controlled up to 100 miles off our coasts, but throughout the entire environment, it seems to me that all nations and all peoples must be alerted to the danger of polluting our environment. In other words, while pollution abatement some 100 miles out to sea may be desirable, the truth is that such a law is unenforceable. To be effective, all nations must be alerted to the need to minimize the waste that they put into the sea. This can only be accomplished by holding an international conference in which all shipping nations participate.
This fact was pointed out by the minister himself when he was asked about the ability of the government to enforce this particular legislation. In response to a question from the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) about enforcing the legislation as it relates to the St. Pierre and Miquelon area, the minister replied that in the case of St. Pierre and Miquelon there is undoubtedly a problem because we would not be able to enforce Canadian law against a foreign owned vessel going to a foreign port. That was one of the unfortunate accidents of geography. The minister went on to say that he hoped that perhaps we could make some kind of practical arrangements with the authorities of St. Pierre and Miquelon because he was sure they did not want to have a major oil spill off their coastline any more than

March 1, 1971

we did. In fact, said the minister, in the one case where this did come up one year we did co-operate with them effectively and in a practical way. In other words, we would be able to enforce the legislation on ships on the high seas destined for a Canadian port, but we could not enforce it on a ship docking at St. Pierre or Miquelon. If that be the case, and I presume the minister had all the facts at this command when he made that statement, it is obvious that the provisions of an amendment of this type giving control over pollution to the Canadian government up to some 100 miles off our shores would be unenforceable.
May I come back to my original suggestion, which is that I believe all nations must be made aware of their responsibilities with regard to pollution. It is for an international conference to alert each and every nation that has ships on the high seas to their responsibility to make certain they do not pollute the high seas.
In closing, and since I see it is almost five o'clock, may I put on the record the facts as stated in a Time magazine article on December 28, 1970 which gives an indication of the sense of responsibility that is now evident among the nations of the world:
In Rome last week, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization tackled the problem-
That is, the problem of pollution.
-by inviting 400 scientists from 40 maritime nations to discuss man s abuse of the seas. The biggest and most important such conference to date produced more than 140 papers describing the danger. For example, two French scientists, Georges Bellan and Jean-Marie Peres, expressed alarm about the Mediterranean. Not only is human waste soiling beaches from Tel Aviv to Trieste, they said, but the "self-cleansing" power of the sea itself can no longer cope with the volume of untreated excrement and industrial waste now pouring into it. As a result, the scientists told their colleagues, "The Mediterranean is rushing toward complete pollution."
Bruce McDuffie, a bearded chemist of the State University of New York at Binghamton, is the man who recently discovered mercury in U.S. canned tuna. In Rome, he reported also finding high mercury levels in commercial swordfish. Reason: according to an American paper presented at the Rome conference, industry is now dumping 5,000 tons of mercury into the oceans each year. Because fish hold mercury in their systems for as long as 500 days, the contamination can travel over vast areas.
Dr. Max Blumer of Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution told the conference that "major catastrophes in production and at sea, unburned fuel, spent lubricants, and a significant hydrocarbon contribution from the land (Municipal wastes) contribute about 10 million tons of oil to the world's oceans each year''. According to Blumer, the immediate effects of oil spills-dead fish and birds- are followed by long-term damage to marine ecology. "Compared to the size of the accidents," he said grimly, "the present countermeasures against oil in the oceans are inadequate.''
The scientists underlined Blumer's hard-hitting report, and scores of others, by recommending an immediate international survey to measure the extent and degree of marine pollution. They also urged establishment of a global monitoring system.
Such a system would involve a fleet of ships and a chain of automatic sensing buoys, plus aerial photography and satellite observation. The system would be used to spot the source of pollutants like oil, mercury and lead. It would also monitor oxygen levels in the seas and "red tides", the abnormal growth of phytoplankton that can choke out other forms of marine life.

Obviously, such a system would need the political support of nations that now exploit and degrade the seas.
That is the best indication I can give that other nations are aware of the problem and are doing something about it. I hope the Canadian government will pursue this matter at the international level, because I believe that only at the international level can we hope to clean up pollution on the high seas. For these reasons, we cannot support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett).

subsubtopic: DESIGNATION OF ELECTORAL DISTRICTS OF BATTLE RIVER AND VEGREVILLE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should immediately amend paragraph (q) of the Schedule to Regional Development Incentives Designated Region Order, 1969-1 to provide that the area comprised by the federal electoral districts of Battle River and Vegreville be designated as a designated region for the purposes of the Regional Development Incentives Act.
He said: In moving this motion to designate the areas of Battle River and Vegreville under the federal regional economic expansion program I am expressing a pressing necessity and, in a formal way, I hope to bring to the minister's attention the deep and urgent need for incentives and supportive industry in these rural areas. Every weekend I go home I find the situation has further deteriorated. Hundreds of farmers and businessmen have already been forced into bankruptcy. Many people who were formerly considered to be well established farmers

March 1, 1971
Regional Development Incentives Act and businessmen now come to me and say it will be only a matter of time until they will be out of business. They can only live on depreciation and credit for so long because the day of reckoning comes. That day is fast approaching for the majority, and a percentage have already gone under.
Last October I made an informal visit to the Department of Regional Economic Expansion to discuss this whole matter. I was informed that there would positively be no redesignation until sometime in 1972. Since that time, however, we have seen an area in southeastern Ontario, and from Montreal to Hull, designated. I am wondering if their situation is really worse than that of certain regions in western Canada. I doubt that this is so. We should always remember that, as agriculture goes, so goes the nation. This has been proven throughout history. There is nothing in our present economic situation which would indicate that this situation will not repeat itself.
Last week some 2,700 employees of Massey-Ferguson were laid off, or there was an indication that they will be laid off. Many thousands more have been laid off in other industries in Canada's industrial heartland. There is nothing we can do for the industrial heartland of Canada which will improve the situation of the employees of Massey-Ferguson. However, if the agricultural industry were functioning as it should be, this situation would not occur. We must give top priority to the agricultural industry and other industries which support it if we are going to get the economy of this country on its feet.
My area of Battle River lies in the heart of the rape-seed area. A crushing and refining plant here, besides employing many people, would enable many more farm families to stay on the farm. Further diversification in respect of a readily saleable crop might be the key, because Canada was a net importer of oil seeds during the past year. If these rural people cannot get the degree of help which might be afforded them by being included as federally designated areas, they cannot help themselves. They are too far run down economically to generate the type of cash which would make it possible to establish plants of this size and description.
We have two designated areas in Alberta. One area exists in the riding of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), the Medicine Hat area. This area, as most Prairie rural areas, should be designated. But I must ask myself why it was chosen over other areas. I have some comparisons of various centres in Alberta. I should like to present them to show the situation which exists in respect of the designated area of Medicine Hat and some of the towns in my riding including Camrose, Stettler, Wainwright, and another area which is not designated, Red Deer. Let us look at the population growth in these areas of my riding. At the outset I must say that they are dwindling. The 1968 figures are the latest I have for five centres including the designated area of Medicine Hat. These figures relate to the capital debt. Medicine Hat had a capital debt of $154 per person. Red Deer had a capital debt of $330 per person, almost double. The town of Wainwright in 1968 had a per capita debt of $195, with Stettler at $172. The latest figures I have for Camrose are for 1970. These figures indicate a capital debt of $270.
Certainly, these figures would substantiate the necessity for designating these areas, particularly if there is justification for designating the Medicine Hat area.
Let us look at the taxable assessment per capita of these areas. In Lethbridge this assessment was, as of 1968, $2,115; in Medicine Hat it was $2,169. These are both designated areas. The taxable assessment in Red Deer for the same period was $1,811; in Wainwright it was $1,471 and in Camrose it was $2,044. For the same period of time the assessment in Stettler was $1,650. There is very little in these statistics which would indicate that these areas should not be designated as well as the area of Medicine Hat which, by the way, is also in my province.
I might refer to the number of building permits issued in order to give a further example of how this area is depressed, in the city of Camrose, in 1967 approximately $4J million worth of building permits were issued and in 1970 the figure was just a shade over $1 million. In the past two years the amount of tax arrears in the county of Camrose has increased by approximately $120,000 to $546,603 as of December 31, 1970. This gives some indication of the number of people who are behind in their taxes. I suggest that unless something is done this property eventually will be taken over by the local governments.
Perhaps we might review the situation by provinces in respect of industrial incentives offered and accepted to illustrate the situation I have just outlined which exists in this western region. I will compare the situations in Alberta and Quebec because I believe this would be as good a comparison as any. Five per cent of the offers under the regional incentives program were accepted for Alberta and 36.5 per cent were accepted for the Province of Quebec. In the time period covered by this graph, 764 new jobs were created in the Province of Alberta and about 7,000 new jobs were created in the Province of Quebec. In respect of the Province of Alberta, 4 per cent of the offers under the regional incentives program were accepted and in respect of the Province of Quebec 35.4 per cent were accepted. If this is truly one nation and all sections are to be dealt with equitably, I fail to see the equity in this situation.
When we consider incentives, we must also consider the matter of freight rates. I mentioned the rapeseed plant and what it would do for our area. Such a plant, however, would be under a handicap from the start. There would be something like a 75 cent a hundred weight handicap on produce coming from this plant, and yet the people of the west pay the full shot of the freight on products produced in the east. I say we must have a review of the freight rate structure in this country if it is truly to be called one nation.
I had occasion to speak to a kindergarten teacher in the city of Camrose who reported that a survey of 25 students in her class shows that 19 of the families were on welfare. There is a terrific reduction of railway employees in this area because of branch line abandonments, stations taken out of operation and consolidation
(Mr. Downey 1
March 1, 1971

of railway facilities. Coal mines for the most part are gone. There has also been a consolidation of the oil production which had developed in some of these smaller areas. Fifteen years ago in the city of Camrose I believe 350 families were engaged in the oil industry, whereas today the number of families is something in the order of ten. This is another indication of what is happening here. People are leaving the area. Where do they go? They merely go on the welfare rolls of the city. If the minister would consider increasing the regional incentives it might be possible for us to attract industry. After all, decentralization is something we must aim for in the future if we are to overcome the pollution problem.
There are predictions that in the cities of the future a third of the population will be engaged in eliminating pollution and looking after the services. I suggest that instead of designating areas which are already industrialized, such as the Montreal area, we would do well to take a look at these rural areas which probably are more in need than many of the areas from which there is a hue and cry. Sometimes it is possible in the agriculture business to hang on a little longer because of government credit programs and so on, but this does not cure the problem.
I draw these things to the attention of the minister. I appeal to the humanity in his soul and ask him to consider these people. Surely, he does not really want to depopulate these areas and have a nation of unemployed people and welfare recipients wandering aimlessly in our urban centres.

speechtext:
If you would listen a little you might get a gleam of an idea. One of the gentlemen who intervened is a member from the east coast. I would think that he and I would be in complete agreement on the way to attack this problem. It would seem to me that he, the hon. member who introduced the motion, myself and many other hon. members from areas that are not in the
Regional Development Incentives Act
very centre of the country have a great deal in common. If we are going to shout across the House at each other, we will never get anywhere. But if we sit down and try to discuss our points of view and how we might approach the problem, it may be possible that several of us together may get an idea that is good enough so that we can sell it to whatever government happens to be in power.
My point is that originally there were two provinces which got a great national idea about 100 years ago. They carried forward that idea, and out of it came Canada. But we have not had a great national idea since. The present government is pledged to the idea of regional equality of opportunity, and I think that what they are doing is great but it is not great enough. It will not give us regional equality of opportunity so long as the criteria on which we work are tied to unemployment figures. The hon. member who introduced this bill knows that the prime problem in both our areas is not unemployment but the movement of people. They move because there are better opportunities elsewhere. Certainly, there are the unemployed and I am not saying there are not, but there are not unemployed in the same sense that there are in other places. The problem on the east coast may again be a different thing. There is chronic unemployment there as well as in some parts of Quebec. We cannot use an omnibus bill based on the criterion of unemployment to solve these different problems. Supposedly, we are all pledged to giving people regional equality of opportunity. I resent the fact that in our province there has to be an exodus of people every year in order for them to have opportunities of employment. It is crazy that they should have to go to Toronto or British Columbia in order to get a job under ordinary circumstances. I am not talking about the time when there is more unemployment everywhere, but under ordinary circumstances this has to be and this does not help federalism.
We are supposed to have regional equality of opportunity. So, I hope that between now and the time when this review takes place we will all address ourselves to the idea of redefining our national dream and how we will achieve a regional equality of opportunity. We cannot come up with an answer indicating that Walter Gordon was right. I do not believe he was right. His idea was to close everything down and move everyone to Ontario because that is where the action is and not to waste our time with the Maritimes, the Prairies and other outlying regions.

They might get back to these regions for a holiday. The answer must lie in a rededication to the national dream of our country for regional equality of opportunity. The CPR would never have been built if Sir John A. Macdonald had used his criterion for solving unemployment in the Prairies. There was no unemployment in the Prairies for the simple reason that nobody lived there, or only 15,000 people. If we do not reverse

the present trend, we will be back to the same position in the next few years.
People leave the Prairies because there is no equality of opportunity. The idea would be to close down the railway as well as all other transportation, and thus save money so that those who live in the centre can enjoy themselves better and be burdened with less taxes. I still say that if we are to have a federal country we must have federal policies which will allow these areas to grow. So, the hon. member who introduced this motion is dead on the mark. I disagree with him because I do not think his motion can work within the criteria of the legislation that exists. I say that we had better change those criteria. If the criteria rests on unemployment alone, every time there is unemployment there will be more unemployment at the centre than at the fringes because more people live there. So, more money will be put in there, and bigger unemployment will follow. I think it is a self-defeating exercise. We have to get the money out into the outlying areas so that the people living there have a fit place in which to live instead of being crowded into the centre and one little valley on the west coast.
This is why I have to admit reluctantly that I cannot support the motion. I think that we should all think of one other aspect, that is that when the time comes for the discussions with the provinces about the revision of this program, which I repeat is only 16 months away, let us do our best to make sure that these talks take place in the open, frankly and freely and that the federal government's policy is made known to everyone. If that takes place, those provinces which are reluctant to make difficult provincial decisions as to where aid is really needed, and where this policy should apply, will not be able to hide any longer behind the excuse that the federal government is reluctant to help them in this or that area. I know of one province-and I am not referring to my own province at present-which said they would just as soon duck the whole business of obtaining any kind of federal aid to improve areas because they did not want to make the difficult political decision as to what areas were or were not to have aid.
I suggest that the federal government should find parameters that are clearly defined so that the next time round the provinces cannot duck these responsibilities and the people will know what we are trying to do. It is up to us as politicians to make sure that the provinces agree with what we are trying to do. I suggest that what we will be trying to do will be to redefine our national purpose and achieve a real equality of opportunity in all areas and regions of Canada.
