speechtext:
I welcome the opportunity of seconding the motion proposed by my colleague, the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Downey) and I welcome the opportunity of participating in the debate. I am sure the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) and for that matter his parliamentary secretary (Mr. O'Connell), will not find it surprising that I wholeheartedly support this motion. I believe they are both very much aware of the continued efforts and representations which I have made to them
regarding the very urgent and pressing need for this kind of program in my area of Alberta.
I do not want to go into detail to reiterate the critical need for supplementing the declining agricultural industry. My colleague, the hon. member for Battle River, has touched on that. I only want to say that in the past three years we have seen net farm income dwindle to an all time low, a figure of $1,325 per farmer in the province, a decrease of more than 50 per cent in the past three years. This comes at a time when the cost of living components are at an all time high. Therefore, it becomes abundantly clear that our economic welfare is seriously impaired to the extent that not only those engaged in agriculture are hurt but those who are engaged in supplying goods and services to the agricultural industry are affected disastrously as well.
It can be said that this government has displayed very capably a lack of dedication and determination to promote and maintain a strong and viable agricultural industry in this country. I submit that it has fallen victim to international pressures, to consumer pressures, and to political pressures, all at the expense of the farmer and of the rural Canadian community. Unless this government rededicates itself to the rural lifestyle based on agriculture, there is very little hope for the survival of many of our smaller, and for that matter larger, rural centres.
Assuming that the government is not determined te look on agriculture as a national asset and hence develop appropriate programs aimed at promoting and maintaining the industry and its people, we are faced with the task of looking for alternatives which must be geared to preserving our rural communities.
Employment opportunities must be provided. A program of diversification is needed. A decentralizing process must take place, and people must be discouraged from flocking to our cities and compounding the problems which exist there. I say that in order to do this we must attract industry to the rural centres and, in Alberta, for example, to centres other than the cities of Calgary and Edmonton. We have a population of over 1J million people in Alberta, over half of them located in those two cities. It is ludicrous to allow this trend to carry on. It is in this tone that I endorse the motion and join in the appeal for serious consideration to be given to the submissions contained in it.
What should be the role of the Department of Rural Economic Expansion in dealing with present developments in rural Canada? Many studies have been made. I refer particularly to the Canadian Council on Rural Development which made some very specific recommendations to deal with the question and put the whole matter of the rural problems of Canada into proper perspective. But we have heard nothing of the minister's reaction to those recommendations, nothing that would lead us to believe that rural development is a priority of the department.

March 1, 1971

I believe that officials of the department have illustrated, both in the past and in the present, that they are dedicated to a program of urban industrialization, without sufficient consideration being given to developing a balanced degree of urban-rural growth. If the department were to consider seriously overcoming the imbalance of rural-urban growth, there is justification for providing industrial incentives to all rural areas of Alberta. I suggest that until the growth and development of rural areas becomes a matter of top priority within the department, the increasing gap between rural and urban dwellers will continue to develop, compounding our social and economic problems. May I simply recall the words of President Nixon when he spoke to Congress early in 1970:
We will carry our concern with the quality of life in America to the farm as well as the suburb, to the village as well as the city.
What rural America most needs is a new kind of assistance. It needs to be dealt with, not as a separate nation, but as part of an over-all growth policy for all America. We must create a new rural environment that will not only stem the migration to urban centres but reverse it.
I think those were well chosen words. They certainly do apply to problems of rural Canada. The purpose of legislation administered under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was adequately spelled out: to assist in the development of Canada, to provide equal opportunity for all Canadians, to overcome slow-growth areas, to provide industrial expansion and to provide jobs.
Time and time again the minister has reiterated the need for a large degree of flexibility to develop the kind of program suited to the specific need. He also stated that common sense and human needs were matters that would be considered as well as statistics and figures when adopting the designated regions; and because he was given large discretionary powers he also stated that he had authority to extend aid to any kind of commercial operation when it was required for the successful development of a special area. It was with this kind of spirit that we as members, and as Canadians, looked forward with anticipation to the implementation of the bill. But what has happened? We have seen the plight of agriculture. The minister has looked upon this as a social problem rather than an industrial problem, suggesting in somewhat evasive terms that a logical solution cannot emanate from the ambit of this act.
The minister cannot understand that agriculture is a basic industry and that when it is adversely affected, correspondingly it affects the welfare and livelihood of practically every citizen living in an area, because their degree of success or failure is commensurate with the success or failure of agriculture. When we consider that every $1 worth of agricultural production has a mulitip-lier effect of $7, it becomes abundantly clear that the vast majority of Albertans are vitally concerned and connected with agriculture. It is with this rationale, I suggest, that the minister should review his position again, particularly in view of the fact that agriculture is not a priority item with the government.
Regional Development Incentives Act
In reply to a letter which I directed to the minister on October 10, 1969, raising objection to the exclusion of the area which I represent, the minister stated that in his opinion a program of incentives to secondary industry would not solve the problems of the rural regions to which I referred. He also said he conceded that there were difficulties facing Prairie agriculture and that appropriate measures would have to be adopted to overcome those difficulties. He said:
This is a matter which we have under discussion with the provincial governments. We are talking about the kind of programs that my department can best employ to ease the necessary adjustment process and cushion its effects on the people of the Prairies.
I am sure I need not remind you, Mr. Speaker, that these discussions have been going on for more than a year and a half, and we are still waiting for such a program. I quote the minister again:
Naturally, there must be increased industrialization on the Prairies if people leaving the farm are to find alternative employment. However, we must face the fact that incentive programs of this kind, no matter how good, cannot attract new plants to every small community.
I do not believe that anyone in this House expects each small community in rural Canada to attract industry. But I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that my area has the kind of communities that could, without difficulty, absorb secondary industry, such as Lloydminster, Yegreville, Vermilion, St. Paul, Smoky Lake, Vilna, Two Hills, Lamont, Mundare Mannville, Tofield and others. These could to good advantage accommodate industries which presently locate in Calgary or Edmonton. These communities have the basic infrastructure, the necessary service facilities, adequate educational, social and cultural facilities tailor-made for medium sized secondary industry. That is what is desperately needed if these communities are to survive and be able to maintain their schools, their roads, their required facilities, their hospitals and all the other things which are necessary components of an adequate standard of living and quality of life, such as cultural, social and recreational institutions.
To the Prairies, and especially to the rural areas, the program of regional economic incentives has been largely a political tool, with the spokesmen of the government paying mere lip service to the real rural problems. The minister gives the impression that his department is not dedicated to the solution of the problems of Prairie rural Canada. However, on the platform he masterfully turns his department into a very useful political selling tool. Here I refer to a speech that the minister made in Meadow Lake, Saskatchewan, early in February when he acknowledged the fact that there are serious problems in the west. However, his speech was full of pious platitudes and consisted basically of political jargon. I submit that if the minister is sincere about coping with the problems, he has within the ambit of the act the necessary framework within which to provide adequate programs to compensate for the problems with which we are now faced.
Adding to the present aggravations is the economic climate which has been developed during the past year

I would like to deal with one such centre which has been dealt a very severe blow, originally because of the department's disregard for much needed assistance to an industry which was an integral part of the community and currently because of the economic climate and the uncertainties which have developed from it. I refer to the community of Two Hills and the phasing-out of the operations of Chemcell Ltd. which provided employment opportunities for some 100 people. The plant there commenced operations in the early fifties. It grew and developed and became a fully integrated part of the community.
In February, 1970, Chemcell announced cutbacks in its operations because of economic circumstances. Also, because new technological methods were discovered, the company would have had to undertake a huge expansion and modernization project in its chlor-alkali operation involving the expenditure of millions of dollars. Because the plan was located on the south bank of the North Saskatchewan River it was ineligible for assistance under ADA. In assessing the situation the company found it could not undertake this massive expansion without some form of assistance and, as a result, decided to phase out that operation, which resulted in the loss of some 30 jobs.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if at this point of time consideration had been given by the government to the matter, it is conceivable that the operation would not only have survived but would have become larger, because there was potential for the manufacture of two other products which would have had the effect of providing more jobs. This in itself has been a serious blow to the people. We now see one year later, on February 23, 1971, that Chemcell announced its intention to close down the plant completely as well as part of its Edmonton operation, causing the loss of some 300 jobs and leaving all those who had been employed in the Two Hills plant jobless. The reasons for the closure were set out in the Edmonton Journal of February 23, 1971, as follows:
The company placed the blame for Its decline in earnings in 1970 on the federal government's anti-inflation measures, continued intense import competition in the chemical fibre and fabric product line, chemical plant problems, escalating costs, the General Motors strike, the unpegging of the Canadian dollar and higher interest costs.
In addition, we were faced with the closing down of the Highland Produce processing plant last summer which employed some 40 native people. That added further to the economic plight of the community. The Highland Produce processing plant was forced to close for economic reasons which were largely prompted by the actions of a vertically integrated co-operative conglomerate. The impact on this community was widespread. The result was some 140 people without jobs in a community of 1,200. If such a rate of unemployment had prevailed in a city like Edmonton, it would have meant that perhaps something like 47,000 people would have been out of work in a community of some 400,000. Surely this is sufficient evidence to establish the need for a positive
course of action to alleviate the hardships of communities such as this. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that under the programs of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and, specifically, of the Regional Incentives Development Act, appropriate measures could be introduced. My hon. friend from Battle River has proposed but one.
I believe that my submissions subscribe to the criteria which the minister said would be paramount in establishing designated regions. These include the human factor, the common sense factor and the statistical factor. I submit that the government ought to take positive action to assist these areas. The present legislation under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion has the required flexibility. It has been demonstrated that the program can meet certain needs. My colleague has mentioned the Montreal and Cornwall areas. The hon. member from the Winnipeg area has suggested that if we adopted this measure, it would water the program down too much. Perhaps the program already has been watered down too much. Nevertheless, certain areas of central Canada still need assistance. The government could act if it wanted to and it should: it has the finances; it has the legislative framework. I suppose its only reservation is what political benefit will accrue to the present administration.

In any event, I should like to support the amendment of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett). I referred to this matter during my speech on second reading of this bill back in October of last year. This is particularly pertinent for a number of reasons which my hon. friend covered at great length this afternoon. I am not prepared to repeat his arguments because I feel he covered the subject comprehensively. He dealt with every possible facet of the bill and I think the House will forgive me if tonight I do not repeat all those arguments.
What concerned us last October, and this concerns us now, is the problem of tremendous ecological violation that might be caused by the spillage of oil through negligence or accident because of the increasing concentration of oil tankers off our shores. I think it might be important to remind the House that the probability of oil tanker spillage is not isolated. Let me document the facts. I am quoting from a publication of the Canadian Scientific Society for Pollution and Environmental Control. It was founded in Vancouver but is now moving toward being a national organization. This publication maintains that while the Torrey Canyon grounding off the British coast, and the Arrow off the Nova Scotia coast, represent tremendous pollution problems, they were not the only ones of importance in the last two years. They were disasters to ecology, but there have been many others.
The brief points out that on February 13, the Delian Apollon struck the side of the ship channel approaching

March 1, 1971
Canada Shipping Act
St. Petersburg, Florida, gashed its hull and released large quantities of bunker C fuel. That was on February 13. On March 3, the 58,000 ton Liberian tanker Oceanic Grandeur was holed in Torres Strait. The report of this Liberian tanker amazed me somewhat because I was not sure they had a marine navy, or whether this involved another matter of international flags of convenience such as the ship off Chedabucto Bay. On May 5, the oil tanker Poly commander caught fire off the coast of Spain and its cargo of 150,000 tons escaped into the sea. The Spanish motorship Monte Ulia rammed a jetty of Mobil's Coryton refinery in the Thames estuary, fracturing a pipeline and releasing 400,000 kilograms of oil into the sea. On October 23, the tankers Pacific Glory and Allegro collided near the Isle of Wight. The Pacific Glory was left stranded, and burned for two days. Also in October, the tanker Manhattan, which is the tanker that attempted to prove the Northwest Passage was usable by tankers, ran aground with a full cargo of 108,000 tons in the Persian Gulf.
The figures I have mentioned document the severity of this problem. We can envisage now the situation we will face with the development of the transshipment of oil by tankers. Obviously it is increasing. More and more people are becoming concerned about this fact. There is a greater army of environmentalists being mobilized to protect what they regard as our ecological future, future life on this planet. This threat has become of greater concern because of public hearings about the proposed Alaskan pipeline from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez. If this is authorized by the Department of the Interior, we will have not just one or two tankers coming down the west coast of Canada but a tremendous concentration.
In supporting the motion of my hon. friend, let me say that the motion implies that if we can keep these tankers far enough off our shores we will have some hope of averting a serious ecological disaster on the west coast. I am sure some hon. members on the other side of the House will say that 100 miles is extending the distance too far out in respect of Canadian sovereignty. Let me point out that this is not an isolated recommendation. Many other spokesmen have suggested that this problem should be viewed in consideration of the danger of disaster to the ecology of our Arctic area. I feel it would be of great service to the world if we moved unilaterally in declaring this kind of standard for our whole coastline as we have for the Arctic. I am convinced that a more moderate ecological zone would be no less sensitive in marine disasters than the Arctic.
In supporting this amendment, I think we are implying the knowledge that there will be disasters as long as oil is transshipped through pipelines to tankers and from tankers to oil refineries. Surely we can maintain sufficient safety standards to ensure that the kind of disaster which will ultimately happen is minimized and delayed as long as possible. We can delay this through rigourous safety standards. Certainly we can ensure that any ship whose cargo is bunker oil is equipped with the proper navigational aids and the kind of internal construction that will minimize the risk to our environment involved
in an oil spill occurring not through an act of God but through negligence or accident.
As Dr. McTaggart-Cowan, who was in charge of the Arrow clean-up pointed out, if we can establish corridors for the transportation of our air traffic, certainly it would be easier to establish similar fixed corridors for the transportation of oil. We should ensure that pilots who are familiar with the region are required, as a matter of course, to make certain that any carrier of this potentially serious kind of pollutant does not take shortcuts and thus incur risks.
Dr. McTaggart-Cowan has a very interesting set of figures which he revealed to this House on November 5, 1970, in his report. Of the need for traffic control, Dr. McTaggart-Cowan says:
The world record is appalling. I have firm figures for the last six months of 1969. Six hundred thousand tons of tanker went to the bottom. That is the equivalent of roughly 33 Arrows-
Mr. Speaker, we are really only beginning to transport oil by tanker. There are some tankers now of 50,000 tons and up to 100,000 tons. There are tankers on the drawing boards which will run as high as 500,000 and 600,000 tons. When we consider the possible devastation, it is no wonder my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni suggests we keep these tankers as far as possible off the Canadian west coast. Someone will say that you can keep them 100 miles off the Canadian west coast, but what will you do when they come into international waters around Puget Sound adjacent to the estuaries of important rivers, notably the Fraser, and probably enter what are the only Mediterranean-type climate seas in Canada? My reply is that we would like to ensure the minimal possibility of damage.
If we have stringent enough regulations in respect of the construction of tankers which travel from Valdez, Alaska, to Cherry Point-if that is where the tankers are to be used-at least we can be reasonably certain that when they get into the international waters of Puget Sound, where devastation could be, to coin a phrase, devastating, at least from that point of view we would have done all in our power to maintain the kind of safety standards which I believe are demanded by this growing threat to marine environment.
We know the minister went to Brussels last year. He was rebuked. The companies which dominate IMCO told him they would not agree to the kind of international convention the minister put forward. The minister came home and said in effect, "We will go it alone". The minister has gone it alone at least out to 12 miles. We would like to see the minister at sea more than 12 miles. We have seen the minister at sea a number of times in this House. We would like to see him much further out, for the reasons I have mentioned.

It is only you people who can walk on the water.

I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that some of us whom the minister regards as lightweights could walk on the water, but there is no possible chance for the minister to walk on the water. His feet are too small, Mr. Speaker.
We know IMCO is dominated by the shipping companies, and we know IMCO will not voluntarily improve the safety standards of the ships of its members. What we need here is a really tough bill. The lobby will come to the committee, as it did, and tell us that if we do this or that we will not get the number of tankers, in the quantities we need for offshore oil, even coming to Canada.
We know perfectly well that if there is a profit to be made, these ships will be here. They will come into Dartmouth, the Burrard Inlet and anywhere they can make a buck. I am quite sure Canada can take a substantial world lead as it did in respect of Arctic sovereignty and the Arctic pollution bill. It can take a tremendous lead in this respect to improve the kind of safety standards available in order to make shipping all over the world more safe. I am not going into the matter of flags of convenience and people hiding behind the same, preventing us from finding out who owns a ship such as the Arrow. I will say, however, in respect of unlimited liability, that shipping companies and insurance companies will not assume the liability. It will be assumed by the general public. If there should be an oil spill off Vancouver Island, guess who will assume the liability?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext: Canada.

Certainly. I am glad to hear from the senator on the other side: he has answered my question. Why should the people of Canada assume that liability? There is no reason for it. Not very many people realize that the world's sea life regenerates on the tide flats and river estuaries and these are precisely the areas which are being most threatened now by the Prudhoe Bay deal. We need a good, tough bill and a good, tough minister who will say he agrees that we need to extend our jurisdiction for pollution control purposes beyond the 12-mile spit that was described earlier today to a reasonable distance so that Canadians can rest assured that their minister, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), of whom they are so proud, will take a leading role in this very important problem.
Mr. Speaker, I know the minister has been convinced, because I saw him attempt to rise a moment ago. I am looking forward to his remarks as soon as I sit down.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to ask some questions of the minister regarding the recent announcement of the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) concerning the 12-mile limit. I will not detain the House long. I want to know from the minister exactly what new government policy has been invoked by the announcement of the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry last Thursday in the
Canada Shipping Act
House when he said the following in reply to a question. I quote from page 3741 of Hansard:
A ruling has been made that all Canadian trawlers must stay outside 12 miles from shore, and this applies particularly off the west coast of Newfoundland. These rules applying to our own trawlers will automatically apply to all foreign vessels as well.
There is a certain amount of misunderstanding in Newfoundland with respect to this question. I am sure the minister has read the Newfoundland weekend papers, as I have, and he will readily admit that the misunderstanding is there. Perhaps this might be a good opportunity to clear up that misunderstanding, because the 12-mile limit issue is relevant to the amendment now before the House; indeed, it is relevant to the whole act since the operative clauses of the act apply within the areas defined as the 12-mile limit.
The question I would put to the minister is: What arrangement has been made with the French authorities with respect to their jurisdiction over the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon? Can we hope there has been agreement with the government of France in this regard? Perhaps, also, he can define what the agreement is and how we get around the fact that the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon are within 12 miles of the coast of Newfoundland at one point, making the drawing of the 12-mile limit following the sinuosity of the coastline almost impossible without some arrangement with the government of France.
There is no question, of course, about the west coast of Newfoundland, and nobody questions it at all; it is a very simple matter. But when you get to the south coast of Newfoundland, taking in most of the minister's own constituency, this is where the problem arises and this is where a great deal of foreign fishing activities take place. This is where the great winter fishery takes place, and this is the area of great difficulty, the one area which poses a real dilemma to the government of Canada with respect to the 1964 statute.
To clear up the misunderstanding that is in my mind at present and which appears to be prevalent in Newfoundland also, perhaps the minister might want to take this opportunity to clarify what seems to be a rather ambiguous situation. My question very simply is: Do we have a 12-mile limit off the south coast of Newfoundland and, if so, what arrangements have been made with the government of France?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as the question of the hon. member relates to fisheries lines and to the whole question of the limit relating to fisheries, it would be more appropriate for the hon. member to put the question to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry, who has responsibility in the matter and who is in day to day touch with it. I have a special and direct concern in so far as the pollution issue is concerned. However, I will try to elaborate and to enlighten the hon. member, with the qualification that I hope he will understand that it is purely and simply a layman's interpretation and that I am merely giving him my understanding of the situation. If it happens that the

March 1, 1971
Canada Shipping Act
legal position is somewhat different, I am sure he and all hon. members will understand.
As to whether or not there is a 12-mile limit off the south coast of Newfoundland, the short answer is yes, for the majority of the distance from, let us say, Cape Ray or Port aux Basques, generally speaking, along the south coast eastward. There is, of course, as the hon. member knows, the geographic problem that roughly speaking off Placentia Bay there are the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon which are the property of France. So that in terms of the area between what might be described as the northern coast of St. Pierre, that is, the coast of St. Pierre nearest to Newfoundland and the southern part of the Newfoundland coast-if my hon. friend can visualize what I mean-according to the conventional way of drawing any sort of national lines or fisheries lines, the distance is equidistant between the two territories which in the event belong to different countries, that is, on the inside part.
So if you can still visualize the map, it would mean that as one approached from the west, coming east along the south coast of Newfoundland at the point where St. Pierre occurs from a geographic point of view, the line would be equidistant between St. Pierre and Newfoundland. This leaves a region on the southern part of the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, and here I would assume-I have to remind hon. members, again, that I am not a legal authority in these matters-that whatever the French government's position is with regard to territorial waters, presumably they would assert that as being their territorial waters in any part of their coastline which did not have a relationship to the coastline of Newfoundland, that is, where the Atlantic Ocean is beyond that. That, as I understand it, is the position, although I do emphasize again that this is purely a laymen's judgment.
On the question of the application of this act in the area relating to St. Pierre, neither I nor, to my knowledge, the government of Canada had any direct negotiations with the government of France with regard to pollution matters. The hon. member may recall that he asked me a somewhat similar question during the second reading of this bill and I replied that we had a more or less ad hoc arrangement with the government of St. Pierre, in the local sense, that we would assist them in the event that there was a pollution problem around their coastline.
I believe basically that is the position as it exists at present. With regard to this measure, I would certainly be prepared, in so far as my own responsibilities extend, to determine whether or not the government of France acting through its representatives on the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon would be interested in making some sort of arrangement with us from a pollution standpoint which would have the effect of closing what is at least a theoretical gap in the lines, although in practical terms it is not my opinion that this would be a serious problem for us in the event of an oil spill in that region.
I say this because I believe common sense would prevail over other considerations and that under the normal rules, if none other than those of decency, we would
assist each other in the event of an oil spill or the threat of an oil spill in that area. But in an effort to formalize such an arrangement I would be quite prepared to explore, through the usual channels of the Department of External Affairs and the government of France, the willingness of that government to work with us jointly on this matter.
I regret that I cannot be more explicit in terms of marine law for the benefit of hon. members, but I hope that what I have said clarifies the matter to some extent. To the best of my knowledge, it does constitute the correct situation.
While I am on my feet, I believe, with regard to the amendment that is before the House, that I cannot do better than reflect the views expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), that is, to say that at present a unilateral decision on the part of Canada to extend its jurisdiction below the sixtieth parallel to 100 miles would be totally unacceptable to the international community. It would not in fact be observed, in our opinion. The wisest course, we believe, is to continue on the way we have been going up to now, and that is to attempt to negotiate with the international community some sort of agreement that will in fact solve the problem which has been quite properly defined by the hon. member who proposed this amendment and by those who have supported it.
There is no question about the fact that it would be advisable and useful to have some form of international agreement to cope with the potential situation to which they have referred. I recall that one hon. member said this afternoon that there is no magic in 100 miles. That is quite true. If we were to have a major oil spill 200, 300 or even 500 miles off our coast, it is by no means inconceivable that the oil could end up right on the coast, ours probably being the longest coastline in the world.
Whilst there may be a certain degree of satisfaction in asserting this form a nationalistic point of view, it is my opinion that it would serve no useful purpose at the present time. Indeed, quite the contrary; I suspect it would slow down significantly the sizeable progress made in the last few months on the matter of international agreements.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, this is probably as good a time as any. As the hon. member will know from following the news for the last six months, there has been a marked softening in the attitude of the shipping

March 1, 1971

nations. Some of it was not reflected in the representations made before our committee, but nevertheless I am quite satisfied that the action taken by the House in giving unanimous first and second reading to this bill has been effective.
There was a clear determination in committee that something must be done in this field. As a result, we have seen initiatives taken by the international oil companies in the form of much larger insurance funds than they held previously. In fact, they have increased their contributions to this pool of money quite significantly and are now prepared to do much more than they were when we went to Brussels in the fall of 1969. In addition, there has been greatly increased activity in the United States in regard to anti-pollution measures. Not only the federal government but several individual states have taken action against this type of threat to the ecology and the shorelines.
For obvious reasons I cannot give particulars, but I can assure the House of a definite movement toward more international co-operation. We have indicated our anxiety to go along with this by establishing bases in this bill which will put us on all fours with the Brussels convention. We are remaining within the international community rather than taking unilateral action. I do not suggest that it is possible or even likely that we will get everything we want within a year or two, but I have not the slightest doubt that the weight of public opinion is with us. I may say that our information indicates some commendation among concerned people in the governments of many countries for the actions we have taken.
I might point out to the hon. member who moved the amendment that his party was dubious about the Arctic sovereignty bill and about the extent to which Canada ought to move unilaterally outside the general framework of international law. At that particular moment it was felt that it was suitable and proper to do so. In a situation such as this I can assure the House that there would be no acceptance. Furthermore, we would be asserting something which would be virtually beyond our power to control.
During second reading in this House and before the committee I pointed out that to extend our territorial waters by 100 miles would be to bisect some of the major shipping lines of the world. Thus we would be asserting our authority over what for many centuries have been established sea lanes. I am not suggesting that there should not be this kind of authority; I am suggesting that we must continue to take the lead to get international agreements to police these sea lanes and to identify routes along which ships such as tankers should be permitted to travel. I believe we will have far more success in this way than if we seek to "do it" alone.
Finally, let me point out that historically the greatest threat is within the territorial waters of a country. There is always the danger of collision at sea, of course, but if one looks at the history of the events to which the hon. member referred, all of them occurred within a comparatively short distance of the shore. In the San Francisco incident the two ships were coming into harbour. We believe that the major threat of accident at the present
Canada Shipping Act
time lies within the 12-mile limit, so I do not feel there is any impediment to effective action in establishing what we have in this bill. I believe this to be entirely defensible in the international community, and I think we should move for the kind of safeguards which I feel are essential but which I feel can only be achieved through international co-operation.

speechtext: Is the House ready for the question? The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that I did not hear all of the minister's statement. I rise for the purpose of saying that I do not think the people on the Pacific Coast will feel too reassured by the statements which have been made by the minister. It is all very well for him to talk about the possibilities of international agreement and of being able to get some satisfactory arrangements made at a conference of the sea. The fact remains that British Columbia faces a very real prospect of a pollution threat if plans are carried out for building the pipeline from the north shore of Alaska to Valdez and transshipping oil from Valdez to Cherry Point, down the west coast of Vancouver island and through the Straits of Juan de Fuca.
The minister may not be satisfied with the amendment. I would have hoped that the minister would himself have asked Parliament to give him and his department adequate powers to deal with this situation. The situation, to some extent, is on a par with the action which the government took one year ago with respect to the Arctic. I refer to the speech which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made in the House of Commons on October 24, 1969. He said, as reported at page 39 of Hansard:
We do not doubt for a moment that the rest of the world would find us at fault, and hold us liable, should we fail to ensure adequate protection of that environment from pollution or artificial deterioration. Canada will not permit this to happen either in the name of freedom of the seas, or in the interests of economic development. We have viewed with dismay the abuse elsewhere of both these laudable principles and are determined not to bow in the Arctic to the pressures of any state. In saying this, we are aware of the difficulties faced in the past by other countries in controlling water pollution and marine destruction within their own jurisdiction.
If the minister has any doubts about the position that this party took with respect to that legislation, he need only look at the record. Our criticism of the government was that it did not immediately concur in the report of the standing committee that had recommended to the House that the government should declare sovereignty not only over the Arctic Islands but the Arctic waters. That was our criticism. We thought the government should have gone further than merely declaring its jurisdiction with respect to pollution control. There can be no doubt about our support for the action which the government took in going as far as it did. We wished it had gone further. Nevertheless, in so far as the government declared that it reserved the right to take the necessary action to control shipping in so far as that shipping might pollute the waters of the Arctic, we supported the government fully.
We think that the same principle ought to apply here. We are not suggesting that the government should have
the right to interfere with the west coast sea lanes. What we are saying is that if oil tankers are to ply the waters between Alaska and the United States, and if they are to pass through Canadian coastal waters and come close to Canadian territory, then the Canadian government should declare, through regulations passed under the Canada Shipping Act, under what conditions those ships will ply those sea routes and what must be the state and condition of the ships as related to the type of cargo.
Ships ought to be required to file the routes which they propose to take, so that in case of fog other ships could be warned as to their location. All the precautions that are possible and need to be taken should be taken to protect the waters off the Pacific coast. Everyone knows, of course, that notwithstanding all the precautions taken, accidents can still occur. The fact remains, nevertheless, that a great many precautions could be taken. Regulations should be enforced. If there are no regulations in this field, conditions imposed will not have any effect.
I do not need to tell the minister about this matter because he knows from experience what happened in Chedabucto Bay. The grounding or sinking of a large tanker anywhere off the west coast of Vancouver Island or in the Straits of Juan de Fuca would pollute that entire area, could destroy one of the most valuable fishing zones in the world and could pollute some of the finest beaches and recreational centres to be found on the North American continent. Surely, therefore, we do not ask too much when we ask that in this legislation there be the necessary powers by which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) can lay down the terms and conditions under which ships carrying pollutants can operate if they are to come within 100 miles of the Canadian western shoreline or if they are destined for ports close to Canada.
The minister says that we will work this out through international law. Yet the fact remains that there is no clearcut international law in this field. The Americans have a three-mile limit; other countries impose limits running all the way from four miles to 200 miles offshore. A wide variety of areas have been established over which coastal states have jurisdiction. As I pointed out in a speech I made last year on the question of sovereignty over the Arctic area, nations in the past who wished to protect their own interests have faced this problem and acted unilaterally. As a result of their acting unilaterally, other nations have followed suit. Then a Conference of the Sea has taken place and a convention has been established. That has happened again and again.
The United States, which might be one of the countries to complain, has again and again taken unilateral action. I think reference has already been made to the Truman declaration of 1945 in which the United States unilaterally declared exclusive control of resources of the continental shelf, which in such cases as the Bering Sea extends for several hundred miles. This proclamation of course did not prohibit ships from sailing in these waters or fishing in them; but it did reserve the resources of the sea bed for the United States for some 250 miles off the east coast and some 60 miles off the west coast of that

March 1, 1971

country. As a result of this action which the United States took on its own initiative, the continental shelf doctrine was accepted by the other nations of the world.
In the same year, the Truman administration in the United States declared that if the United States of its own initiative decided to exercise the right to regulate and control the fishing industry for purposes of conservation, then it had that right even on certain areas of the high seas where other nationals were fishing. It maintained and exercised that right. As a matter of fact, before the United States became a great oil shipping nation, as far back as 1926 that country proposed at a Conference of the Sea a convention which would prohibit the discharge of oil into the sea. Later, the United States began to ship oil. It objected when other nations wanted to impose this type of prohibition. I point these things out merely to suggest to the minister that if he is going to be timid and wait until there is international agreement, until somebody else takes the initiative and until there is finally a Conference of the Sea, he may wait for a long time.
In the meantime, the people of British Columbia may be the victims of the government's hesitancy. We are appealing to the minister to assume these necessary powers now. We have sufficient confidence in the minister that he will not exercise these powers in an arbitrary manner and upset shipping on the high seas. The minister should seek the necessary authority in Parliament to declare that Canada will impose conditions by regulation to which ships carrying oil or other pollutants coming close to the Canadian coastline must abide. That is all. Surely the minister needs some kind of powers to do that.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext: Do you consider 100 miles to be close?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext:
I consider that 100 miles is a reasonable area. Possibly the minister thinks that 50 miles is more reasonable and wants to suggest that. Ships will come down from Alaska, go out past the west coast of Vancouver Island and then have to swing in around Canadian territory to get to Cherry Point. The minister ought to have some power to exercise control over those ships.
It is no secret that some oil tankers operated under the flags of various nations are not the most seaworthy vessels. I have seen some come into the harbours in my constituency where it was possible to knock out part of the bulkhead with a hammer because they were so rusty, old and decrepit. How seaworthy are they? How safe are they to be sailing our waters, when if they begin to leak they could pollute the entire coastline and destroy the livelihood of the fishermen on the west coast of British Columbia?
If the minister is not prepared to accept this amendment, I hope he will be prepared to suggest the kind of powers which he thinks he requires in order to keep the danger of polluting the west coast of Canada to a minimum. No one can guarantee we will not have any pollu-
Canada Shipping Act
tion as a result of an accident at sea, but there could be regulations regarding the seaworthiness and condition of ships, navigational aids, filing of the route they are going to follow and a series of provisions that would at least reduce the hazard and thereby lessen the risk.
I think the minister ought to be prepared to at least do that. If he is not going to do it, he must accept the responsibility if in one, two or three years there is a major wreck of an oil tanker or some other catastrophe on the west coast of British Columbia. That is a responsibility which I, personally, would not want to assume. I do not think the minister is going to be burdened by asking Parliament for this authority. He can then sit down with his officials and with those who are knowledgeable on this subject to work out the kind of regulations which would be necessary to keep to the absolute minimum the danger of pollution from a wreck.
I hope the minister will be prepared to reconsider his decision, be bold and take the initiative in declaring Canada's right to exercise jurisdiction and control in so far as controlling pollution is concerned. I am convinced that if the minister takes that bold action, not only Canadians but other coastal states will support him. In time we will have a Convention of the Sea which will endorse the position the minister should be taking. Surely it would be better for the minister to take the initiative than to placidly wait until somebody else manages to persuade the other coastal states to agree to such a measure.
The government had the courage to declare its authority with respect to pollution control in the Arctic. Surely it is equally important, if not more important, that it exercise the same jurisdiction with respect to the much more settled areas of Canada, namely, the Atlantic and Pacific coastlines.

speakeroldname: Mr. Louis-Roland Comeau (South Western Nova) moved:
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DISCHARGE OF POLLUTANTS BY SHIPS
speechtext:
That Bill C-2, to amend the Canada Shipping Act, be amended in clause 2 by striking out the word "oil" on line 36 at page 23, lines 1, 12, 14, 16, 19, 26, 29, 30, 33 and 38 at page 24, and lines 11, 30 and 33 at page 25 and substituting therefor the word "pollutant".
He said: Mr. Speaker, this amendment is quite simple. It merely changes the word "oil" to "pollutant". Hon. members who have not followed the committee's reports will, I am sure, agree that it sounds quite simple. Frankly, it is simple. The amendment I moved this afternoon was accepted by the minister. I hope this amendment receives the same treatment.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that money is required to fight pollution. The amendment deals specifically with the clause which relates to the maritime claims fund. While I was absent from the proceedings in the committee on February 11 the chairman introduced a couple of amendments and described them as a joint effort of myself and another member. This is one of them. It was moved in the committee but the committee chose to accept one which provided that the Governor in Council might make regulations prescribing pollutants other than oil. This is well and good.
* (9:10p.m.)
We have had experience of certain pollutants which are, or could be, detrimental to our waters. Nevertheless, the regulations have not yet been brought forward. At least, this was the situation on February 11. But the whole bill depends upon regulations of some sort, regulations with respect to ship construction, the security of tanks used to transport liquids, and so on. In consequence, we do not yet know what substances the government considers to be pollutants and what it does not.
As I say, money is needed to fight pollution. The government therefore proposes to set up a fund which could be used to clean up whatever mess is caused should there be an accident or incident. Most of the witnesses who appeared before the committee expressed concern about this clause, about the proposed levy and about the claims fund. They feared that if the levy were set too high, the companies concerned would simply pass the costs over to the consumers.
I am surprised that more attention has not been paid to this bill, since it is a measure which affects international interests. It is proposed to place a levy upon oil or other pollutants and, as we know, our imports and exports are carried almost entirely by foreign vessels in the absence of what might be called a viable Canadian shipping industry. Sections of the oil industry have expressed their concern about the provisions dealing with the claims fund and it may be the levy will be detrimental to Canadian industry. In these circumstances we should take a close look at the clause before us.
I do not believe the blame for pollution should be laid entirely on the oil industry. In the last year or so there have been cases of pollution by phosphorous, for example. Phosphorous is being transported in Canadian
waters. Insecticides and pesticides are being transported through Canadian waters, not only in the Pacific and the Atlantic but the Great Lakes. Thus, there are other pollutants which should be required to bear a portion of this charge; the levy should not be limited to oil. I refer to an incident on the St. Lawrence close to Montreal last year which caused some alarm.
The argument used in committee against this amendment was a simple one. Hon. members will find it stated on page 1563 of the committee report for February 11. Mr. Macgillivray was answering for the department; he was really the only departmental witness, because the minister only attended once and the parliamentary secretary did not become a witness. When we asked whether pollutants other than oil should not also be the subject of a levy in connection with the fund, Mr. Macgillivray suggested it was not very practicable because the amount of the levy could not exceed 15 cents per ton. The committee eventually accepted a compromise of sorts to the extent that pollutants could be prescribed by regulation.
As the bill is presently written, it seems to me there is no limit to the size of the fund which could be built up, nor do we know how large a sum the government will require. When, if ever, will it cease collecting this levy of 15 cents per ton? Would it be suspended if, for example, it were found that sufficient funds had been accumulated to take care of any spill which might reasonably be expected? I should like to know whether this is being kept in mind, because in these hard times there is no need to tax industry too heavily simply for the sake of doing so, especially if there is to be a detrimental effect upon the Canadian economy.
I find it hard to argue this amendment. If I argue too strongly in favour of it, hon. members will think I am not really interested in protecting the environment but am more interested in protecting the interests of industry. But it seems to me there must be a reasonable balance somewhere; we cannot always kick industry around. In other words, we must take some responsibility.
Let me look at some of the funds presently in existence. Other funds have been set up for the same purpose as the maritime claims fund; for example, there is the CRISTAL fund, and there is also TOVALOP. On January 14, 1971, the Oil Companies Institute for Marine Pollution Compensation Limited issued a press release dealing with this problem. Perhaps Your Honour will permit me to read a couple of paragraphs so that the House knows what these funds involve:
A number of leading oil companies of the world signed a voluntary agreement in New York today-
That was on January 14, one month ago.
-as a further step by the industry to help fight pollution of the oceans from oil spills from tankers and at the same time announced formation of an institute to administer it. The agreement supplements ship owners' liability by providing for com-

March 1, 1971

pensation up to $30 million per incident involving participating companies and is expected to become effective April 1st.
The newly formed Oil Companies Institute for Marine Pollution Compensation Limited would administer the funds contributed by participating oil companies. These funds would be used to compensate claimants for oil pollution damage beyond the liability of tanker owners, including reimbursement of the cost of cleaning up such oil spills.
Today's agreement, known as CRISTAL (Contract Regarding an Interim Supplement to Tanker Liability for Oil Pollution), supplements a previous anti-pollution insurance program in which tanker owners participate. The earlier agreement, known as TOVALOP (Tanker Owners Voluntary Agreement Concerning Liability for Oil Pollution), was signed in 1969 and imposed responsibility upon participating tanker owners for reimbursing governments to a maximum of $10 million per incident for cleaning up of oil spills. TOVALOP covers over 80 per cent of the world's tanker tonnage.
Thus, in the case of an oil spill from a TOVALOP tanker, CRISTAL will supplement the tanker owner's responsibility to an over-all total of $30 million provided the cargo belongs to a participating company.
So there are funds in existence at the moment and most oil companies participate in them. The problem is that the compensation comes from one source only; you cannot claim compensation from several sources. The CRISTAL agreement to which I referred a moment ago provides that where national funds are established-for example, the maritime claims fund-compensation is available only to the extent that the national fund is unable to cover the cost.
Thus, if the proposed maritime pollution claims fund were established in Canada, financed by Canadian oil companies and hence indirectly by Canadian consumers, Canada would be denying herself the full benefits of the other funds, CRISTAL and TOVALOP, the financing of which will be contributed to on a worldwide basis, not only by Canadian industry. Therefore, it seems to me that under these circumstances it becomes highly questionable whether the establishment of this fund is in Canada's best interests. I am not saying that a fund should not be set up; I am just pointing out some of the matters, that give me concern, without taxing industry to the extent that it cannot cope. There was some evidence in the committee that industry cannot cope. I know one company in New England has been talking about levying a charge of 3 per cent, whereas others have thought of levying a charge of 15 cents per ton of oil carried. If a Canadian company is called upon to pay 15 cents a ton as well as three cents at a U.S. port, then quite frankly I do not know how the industry will manage.
The word "pollutant" as a general term is well defined in the definition clause of this bill. I suggest that if the amendment were accepted we would be able to increase the fund. However, after it reaches a certain limit I would hope contributions would cease or, failing that, at least the levy would be reduced to ease the burden on industry. I realize that this fund needs to be built up quickly in case a spill occurs next year, for example. As far as the famous Arrow incident on the east coast is concerned, the minister has mentioned that Canada was billed for something like $2 million to $3 million and I presume we are going to be taxed for that bill. I wonder
Canada Shipping Act
why this is necessary since TOVALOP was in existence at that time and now there is CRISTAL. Why did the government not ask the company involved, which I am sure belongs to this fund, to pay for the cost of cleaning up this oil spill, rather than asking Canadian taxpayers to foot the bill?
The argument that we will not be tagged again with this type of bill does not stand alone; the great majority of oil companies belong to one of the two funds to which I have referred. I hope that the minister will consider this amendment and accept it. Failing that, I trust he will assure the House that the consumers of this country will not again have to bear such an expense. If the cost of cleaning up a spill is too high, this is what will happen.
As I mentioned, the amendment would have the effect of increasing the fund at an accelerated rate. This fund should be reviewed, as suggested before the committee by Mr. Macgillivray, after a certain length of time. Once the fund reaches a certain limit I would hope that the levies would be suspended or at least reduced. If there is no accident for 20 years and we keep collecting this money, the government will put it into the consolidated revenue fund and it will be used for something else. We have seen this happen too often in respect of other funds and pension schemes. The government has used such money for other purposes.
In this case we should not allow the government to use this fund for any reason other than that for which it was designed. I hope the government will look favourably on this amendment in view of the fact that it touches upon the whole topic of maritime trends. Once this measure becomes effective and the fund begins to grow, I hope the government will realize that there are pollutants other than oil which may be as dangerous to our environment. We all know what happened last year in respect of phosphorous. There was a big fuss in this House a year and a half ago about the danger of this pollutant. It seems to me that cargoes of this kind of pollutant should be taxed in the same way in which we propose to tax oil cargoes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment of the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) and the arguments he has advanced have the virtue of making at least one point clear. After this bill is passed and becomes operative, members of the House will have a continuing responsibility to observe and examine the administration of the regulations this government enacts, in order to satisfy themselves that they are being applied in such a way as to avoid seriously and unnecessarily interfering with the operation of trade and commerce in Canada while at the same time preventing pollution.
This is particularly true because of the authority placed in the Governor in Council to adopt regulations as it sees fit. The hon. member has related his amendment to the question of revenues and has suggested that in some way his amemdment would make the operation and maintenance of the fund relevant to an appropriate level.

March 1, 1971
Canada Shipping Act
Quite frankly, I fail to follow his argument in this connection.
There were suggestions made by members of the committee, including myself, that provision should be made in the bill for the inclusion of substances other than oil to be classed as pollutants and considered liable for charges and payment to the fund. It seems to me that the basic point of the hon. member's amendment is covered by the amendment of the committee now before the House. This amendment to proposed section 758 is to be found at page 25 of the bill returned from the committee. It seems to me that the hon. member's amendment is unnecessary and irrelevant, and for that reason I would argue against it. If his amendment were to pass, it would mean there might be a levy of 15 cents per ton, or some lesser rate if the government saw fit to set it at a lesser level, in resepct of every kind and class of substance that might be declared to be a pollutant.
This matter was discussed in the committee and it was suggested that under certain circumstances this would be quite inappropriate. After listening to the evidence presented to the committee, I was convinced that there may be some pollutants declared under the legislation in respect of which the appropriate charge to the fund could well amount to $15 per ton rather than 15 cents. I have in mind highly toxic substances, much more pollutant than oil, which may be carried in smaller quantities at a higher level of taxation. They might be taxed at a higher level in order to cover the greater risk to our ecological resources.
The member suggests that the regulations are not enacted as yet and we do not know what they will be. I should like to have seen the regulations before we considered this bill. We often run into this old argument which is akin to the chicken and the egg dispute. We request details of regulations before we give approval to a bill. Had there not been an agreement in the committee in respect of provisions to levy charges on the transportation of other pollutants, I could see some point in the hon. members' amendment or some modification of it. As the matter stands, it seems that this amendment is unnecessary and would only confuse the issue. Therefore, I feel I cannot support it. I suggest to the House that it should not accept the amendment.
The hon. member has suggested that as a result of the assessment of charges under this measure there would be an accumulation of a great deal of funds. As far as I was able to ascertain, no one with knowledge of these matters, either from the department or other experts, was able to suggest what should in fact be the maximum. I am satisfied, under the circumstances, to allow a certain amount of accumulation and let experience be the guide as to the permissible level of this fund, before any reduction in the levy is considered. I do not think the hon. member's argument in respect of this proposed section is relevant to the practical situation. If his amendment were adopted, I do not think it would contribute to making the administration of the legislation easier than it will be as the bill stands.
